sections.label: The opening
sections.line: The 2018 book, an AI edition, made first
sections.para: Dinis's 2018 book Generation Z Developers is on Leanpub at 60% and on Amazon, with 90 of 138 files still outlines that newsroom articles now answer. Generation Z Developers (AI edition) keeps the name, dated October 2026, frames readers as explorers, villagers or town planners, and is the first book made this way: review, an editor interviewing Dinis, public iterations, KDP.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Keep the name, frame it, do it first
sections.para: Written in 2018 and left 60% complete, the book holds many current ideas as outlines that articles now answer. The new edition keeps Generation Z Developers, dated October 2026, uses Wardley's explorers, villagers and town planners as its frame, and goes first: review, interview, iterate in public, publish on KDP, launch in Portugal.

sections.label: The book
sections.line: Generation Z Developers, as it stands
sections.para: Subtitled key concepts and ideas for the next generation of developers, it is on Leanpub at 60% complete, 136 pages and 30,695 words, last updated on 8 October 2018 with 465 readers, also on Amazon, with its source on GitHub. It was written in Markdown, in Git, in public, with GitHub issues for feedback; decent, unfinished and full of spelling mistakes.

sections.label: What it said
sections.line: One competitive advantage, and act like part of the company
sections.para: The book worried that Generation Z, born after 1996, had missed how technology came to work. Its job chapter said the best way to get a job is one competitive advantage, once using a computer or the internet, and to act like part of the company by collaborating on its open source. It also said to learn AI within five years; ChatGPT came four years later.

sections.label: What held, and what did not
sections.line: What held and what did not
sections.para: Held: one competitive advantage, now agentic workflows; act like part of the company; publish; GitHub as your CV; your future self; pioneers, settlers and town planners. Did not: the dated list of tools to learn; the advice to learn how to program AI, when using and directing it mattered more; and a narrow idea of who counts as a developer.

sections.label: The outlines have been written
sections.para: Of the 138 files, 90 are outlines, including all eight on security and 26 of 27 on concepts. Many read like briefs the newsroom later wrote without planning it: future self as bringing my past work back, publish as your own newsroom, graphs as the graphs books, GitHub as your CV as act as the job you want. Written chapters have newer answers too.

sections.label: The cover
sections.para: The printed early release of September 2018 lists seven aims on its cover: question everything, make fact based decisions, understand the history of tech, learn how to learn, understand what game is being played, develop intellectual curiosity, shake things up. Dinis would keep all seven, which read more urgently now.

sections.label: The name
sections.line: Developers, because they all have to create
sections.para: Dinis considered Generation AI developers, professionals or workers, and kept developer: this generation all have to create. In 2018 the book said learn Git, spreadsheets, automation and Slack, but the bar of entry was high; now it is low, and the book could be handed to Claude to teach someone. The new edition is marked (AI edition) and dated October 2026.

sections.label: Explorers, villagers and town planners
sections.para: If everyone is a developer, the question is what kind. Simon Wardley's pioneers, settlers and town planners, renamed explorers, villagers and town planners in 2023, give the book its frame: where you fit and where you want to. The 2018 book had this as an outline; the new one can explain Wardley maps properly, with visualisations.

sections.label: The AI edition
sections.para: Start with a thorough review, spelling first. Keep what held, add then and now for what changed, fill outlines from the articles, add parts on working with agents and on how the book itself was made, use many figures and experiments, and include the handwritten notes from Dinis's printed copy, or fresh comments if it cannot be found.

sections.label: Why this one first
sections.para: There are other books to do, on the graphs among them, but this one has enough material and is already published, so it can be fixed, improved and released as a new version on Amazon. It is a focused target for quick iterations; if the workflow works, Hacking Portugal can follow. And it is the book Dinis wants to hand to people he meets.

sections.label: How it gets made
sections.line: A repository, roles and an editor who interviews
sections.para: A new repository maps the workflow as it runs. A reviewer, editor and publisher reuse the roles and tools from graphs.sgit.ai. The editor interviews Dinis and challenges him, as Claude did for ten hard questions for RiskMandate. Versions go to Leanpub and LinkedIn for feedback, then to KDP, with Web Summit in Lisbon as a launch.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: A plan, with its readings marked
sections.para: Nothing of the AI edition is written, and the outline-to-article map is a first reading. Doing this book first is a choice, with the graphs books and Hacking Portugal to follow if the workflow works. Fear about AI among young Europeans is Dinis's reading, not a measurement. The Amazon listing was not read.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Leanpub, the repository, a photo and two memos
sections.para: From two voice memos of 18 October 2026, the book's Leanpub page and repository, every file counted, and Dinis's photo of the printed early release. Also Simon Wardley's 2015 and 2023 posts on the three roles, the ten hard questions interview as the method, and graphs.sgit.ai's roles.
